(CNN) -- The bodies of young elephants covered in the brown dirt of dried-up wells tell a heartrending story. A baby elephant in the Gourma region of central Mali had been trapped in a well for three days. Reaching desperately for drops of water, they had lowered their trunks, toppled in, remained trapped and died in Mali's scorching heat. The "last desert elephants in West Africa" have "adapted to survive in the harsh conditions" they face, Save the Elephants said Monday. But now, the group says, conditions have gone from bad to worse, and they are living "on the margin of what is ecologically viable." Save the Elephants distributed new pictures Monday that depict the devastating drought and the struggle for survival in Mali, one of the poorest nations in the world. "Six elephants have already been found dead," the group wrote in a news release accompanying the photos. "Four others, including three calves, were recently extracted from a shallow well into which they had fallen when searching for water. Only the largest survived." The youngest are in the most danger, since their smaller trunks can't reach deep into the few remaining wells, the group said. The worst drought in 26 years is threatening the existence of the "last desert elephants in West Africa," the northernmost herds in the continent, Save the Elephants said. The animals, now numbering only about 350 to 450, have been called "the last elephants of Timbuktu," said Jake Wall, a scientist with Save the Elephants. But they're south of Timbuktu, Wall told CNN in a phone interview from Bamako, Mali. "We tend to refer to them as 'the last Sahelian elephants.' "  See a map of Mali » . Each year, the elephants trek farther on the fringes of the Sahara to find water. They have the longest migration route of any in the continent, traveling "in a counterclockwise circle" of about 700 kilometers (435 miles), Save the Elephants said. The images are signs of the crisis gripping the northwest African nation. The U.N. Development Programme ranks Mali near the bottom of its Human Development Index. It cites a 56 percent poverty rate in the country, with nearly a third of the population unlikely to live past age 40, and an illiteracy rate of 77 percent. The World Food Programme says the majority of infant deaths in Mali are due to malnutrition. The drought, combined with soaring temperatures, has also led to deaths of cattle, Save the Elephants said. "The stench of rotting corpses fills the air, and what little water remains is putrid and undrinkable by all standards." In areas where the elephants live and search for water, "the normal peaceful coexistence between the elephants and herdsmen is starting to break down and giving way to conflict over access to water," Wall said. There is some hope for the weeks and months ahead. "We're hoping the rains start in June, and that will allow the elephants to start drinking out of shallow ponds until the really heavy rains begin" in July or August, Wall said. But "urgent action" is needed in the interim "to secure water for the elephants," Wall's group said in its news release. Save the Elephants, which focuses on helping elephant populations worldwide, said it has partnered with a foundation and the Mali government in its fundraising appeal.

# Last of Mali's Desert Elephants Face Extinction as Historic Drought Grips the Sahel

*Conservationists warn that one of the world's most remarkable elephant populations may not survive worsening climate conditions*

---

**GOURMA REGION, Mali** — In the parched expanses of central Mali, where the Sahara Desert bleeds into the semi-arid Sahel, one of nature's most extraordinary survival stories is reaching a devastating chapter. The famed desert elephants of Gourma—among the last of their kind on Earth—are dying as one of the region's worst droughts in decades depletes the scarce water sources they depend on.

## A Remarkable Population Under Threat

The Gourma elephants are unlike almost any other on the continent. Numbering only in the few hundreds, they have adapted to survive in one of the harshest environments any elephant population endures, undertaking one of the longest known elephant migrations in Africa—a grueling circular route of roughly 300 miles in search of water and forage.

"These are some of the most resilient elephants in the world," said a spokesperson for Save the Elephants, the Kenya-based conservation organization that has tracked the population for years. "They have survived in conditions that would be unimaginable for other herds. But there are limits to what any animal can endure, and prolonged drought pushes them past those limits."

## Vanishing Water in a Warming Land

The Gourma region receives minimal annual rainfall, and the elephants have historically relied on a network of seasonal lakes and waterholes—most critically Lake Banzena. But successive failed rainy seasons have left these vital sources dry or badly diminished.

As temperatures climb and water disappears, elephants weakened by dehydration and hunger have been found dead along their migratory paths. Calves and older animals are especially vulnerable.

"When the water disappears, the elephants must walk farther and farther, expending energy they cannot afford to lose," the Save the Elephants representative explained. "We are seeing animals collapse from exhaustion before they reach the next water source. It is heartbreaking to witness."

## Conflict and Climate: A Deadly Combination

The elephants' plight is compounded by the region's chronic instability. Central Mali has been wracked by armed conflict and insecurity for years, severely limiting the ability of conservationists and rangers to monitor herds, provide emergency support, or combat poaching.

"The security situation makes everything more difficult," the spokesperson noted. "In a stable environment, we might be able to intervene—to help protect remaining water sources or guide communities in coexistence efforts. But access is dangerous and, in many areas, impossible."

Local communities, themselves struggling with the drought's impact on their livestock and crops, find themselves competing with elephants for the same dwindling resources—a tension that can turn deadly for both people and animals.

## A Broader Warning

Scientists point to the Gourma elephants as a stark example of how climate change is reshaping the survival prospects of wildlife across the Sahel, a region on the front lines of global warming.

"What is happening to these elephants is a warning," said the Save the Elephants spokesperson. "The Sahel is warming faster than the global average. If we lose the Gourma elephants, we lose not just a population, but a symbol of adaptation and resilience—and a piece of natural history that can never be recovered."

## Racing Against Time

Conservation groups continue to call for international attention and support, including efforts to secure water access, stabilize the region, and integrate elephant protection into broader humanitarian and climate resilience programs.

For now, the fate of Mali's desert elephants hangs in the balance—a living testament to survival against the odds, facing perhaps their greatest challenge yet.

"We have not given up," the spokesperson said. "But time is running out, and the rains have not come."

# West Africa's Northernmost Elephant Herds Face Extinction as Worst Drought in 26 Years Grips the Sahel

**By Staff Correspondent**

## Ancient Migratory Herds Push to the Brink

In the arid borderlands of central Mali, one of the most remarkable elephant populations on Earth is fighting for survival against a drought that regional experts describe as the most severe in more than a quarter century.

The Gourma elephants, which range across the Sahel in what constitutes the northernmost elephant population in Africa, have long adapted to one of the harshest environments any elephants inhabit. But this year's failed rains have stretched their legendary resilience to a breaking point.

These elephants undertake one of the longest migratory routes of any elephants in the world—an annual circular journey covering roughly 300 miles—following ancient pathways in search of water and forage across the semi-desert landscape shared by Mali and Burkina Faso.

## A Population Already Under Siege

Conservationists estimate that only several hundred of these elephants remain, a fragile number that leaves the population acutely vulnerable to any additional pressure. Decades of poaching, habitat fragmentation, and encroaching human settlement had already thinned their ranks before the current climatic crisis.

"When you are dealing with a population this small, every animal matters enormously," said one wildlife biologist familiar with the region. "A drought of this magnitude doesn't just kill individual elephants—it threatens the genetic viability of the entire herd. Once you lose breeding females and their calves, recovery becomes extraordinarily difficult."

The youngest and oldest elephants are the most susceptible. Calves that cannot keep pace with the herd as it travels farther in search of shrinking water sources often perish, while aging matriarchs—repositories of the ancestral knowledge that guides the herd to remembered water holes—weaken under the strain.

## The Drought's Devastating Reach

The failed rainy season has dried up seasonal lakes and waterholes that the elephants depend upon during the punishing dry months. As natural water sources evaporate, the animals are forced into ever-closer contact with human communities that are themselves struggling to survive.

This convergence at dwindling water points creates a dangerous flashpoint. Herders bringing thirsty cattle to the same shrinking pools compete directly with elephants for a resource that has become precious beyond measure.

"The drought compresses everything—people, livestock, and wildlife—into the same shrinking spaces," an environmental researcher noted. "That competition breeds conflict, and in a conflict between a farmer's livelihood and an elephant, the elephant usually loses."

## A Backdrop of Human Hardship

The elephants' struggle unfolds against one of the world's most challenging human landscapes. Mali ranks among the poorest nations on the planet, consistently placing near the bottom of the United Nations Human Development Index.

A substantial share of Mali's population lives below the international poverty line, subsisting on less than a few dollars per day. The country's economy remains heavily dependent on agriculture and livestock—precisely the sectors most devastated by drought. When rains fail, families that were already food insecure are pushed into acute crisis.

Life expectancy in Mali falls well below the global average, and access to clean water, healthcare, and education remains limited across vast stretches of the rural interior where the elephants roam. The Sahel region as a whole faces chronic food insecurity, with millions of people requiring humanitarian assistance in difficult years.

These overlapping human pressures complicate conservation. In a region where families struggle to feed their children, asking communities to prioritize elephant protection over immediate survival presents an extraordinary dilemma.

## The Security Dimension

Compounding the ecological and economic crises is a persistent instability across central and northern Mali. Insecurity in the region has hampered conservation monitoring, made anti-poaching patrols dangerous, and disrupted the delicate community relationships on which elephant protection depends.

Conservation workers face significant risks operating in areas where armed groups are active, and the breakdown of governance in some districts has created openings for poachers seeking ivory.

## Expert Voices Urge Action

Specialists working to protect the Gourma elephants emphasize that their survival is inextricably linked to the wellbeing of local people.

"You cannot save these elephants by fencing them off from the communities they live alongside," one conservation expert explained. "The only durable solution is one where local people see tangible benefit from the elephants' presence—where protecting wildlife and improving human livelihoods become the same project rather than competing priorities."

Community-based conservation initiatives have sought to enlist local residents as guardians of the herds, providing employment and building local investment in the elephants' future. Advocates argue that such programs, though modest, offer the most realistic path forward.

"These elephants have survived in this landscape for thousands of years," the expert added. "They have adapted to drought, to heat, to scarcity in ways that would kill other elephant populations. But they cannot adapt to everything at once—drought, human pressure, and instability together. That combination is what we fear most."

## An Uncertain Future

As the dry season deepens, the fate of West Africa's last northern elephants hangs in the balance. Whether the herds can endure until the next rains—and whether those rains will come in sufficient measure—remains unknown.

For conservationists and the communities of Mali's Gourma region alike, the coming months represent a test of survival shared across species. The outcome will reveal whether one of Africa's most extraordinary wildlife populations can persist in an increasingly unforgiving world—or whether the drought of this generation will mark the beginning of their end.

*A journalistic feature examining the intersection of wildlife conservation and human survival in the Sahel*

---

In the arid expanse of central Mali, where the Sahara's edge meets scattered acacia woodlands, one of Africa's most remarkable elephant populations undertakes an epic journey for survival. But increasingly, that journey is ending in tragedy for the herd's most vulnerable members.

## The Longest Migration

Mali's desert elephants, numbering only a few hundred, are among the last of their kind. These animals travel the longest migration route of any elephants on Earth—a punishing circular path spanning hundreds of kilometers across the Gourma region as they search for water and forage in one of the planet's harshest environments.

Their survival is a testament to endurance. These elephants have adapted to endure temperatures and drought conditions that would prove fatal to their savanna cousins, moving in a seasonal rhythm dictated entirely by the availability of water.

## A Deadly Hazard

Yet water itself has become a source of danger. Across the migration corridor, communities have dug wells to sustain their livestock and families. For adult elephants, these open pits pose little threat. But for calves—curious, small, and less sure-footed—the wells can become death traps.

Baby elephants, unable to climb out once they tumble in, face a desperate struggle. Some perish before they can be found. Others are discovered too late, having exhausted themselves against the steep, unforgiving walls. For a population already so small, the loss of each young elephant represents a serious blow to the herd's long-term future.

## Where Conservation Meets Crisis

Understanding this crisis requires acknowledging its human dimensions. The Gourma region sits within a broader zone of instability, where a humanitarian emergency has unfolded alongside the conservation challenge.

Insecurity, poverty, and the pressures of climate change have strained communities that share this landscape with the elephants. Water is scarce and precious for everyone. The wells that endanger elephant calves are lifelines for people and their herds—a reminder that conservation cannot be separated from the welfare of those who live alongside wildlife.

Conflict in the region has complicated efforts to monitor and protect the elephants, at times making fieldwork dangerous or impossible. In this fragile context, the fate of the elephants and the fate of the people are deeply intertwined.

## The Path Forward

Conservation organizations, including Save the Elephants, have long emphasized the importance of understanding elephant movements to protect them. By tracking migration routes and identifying the points where elephants and human infrastructure collide, conservationists hope to reduce preventable deaths.

Solutions being considered range from modifying dangerous wells to fostering coexistence strategies that benefit both people and elephants. Community engagement is central: local people who understand the value of the elephants—and who see their own needs respected—become the most effective guardians of the herd.

For Mali's desert elephants, the challenge is stark. Their extraordinary migration has carried them through centuries of hardship. Whether it can carry them through this era—marked by conflict, climate stress, and the hidden dangers of the wells—may depend on the ability of humans to protect the youngest travelers on this ancient route.

---

*By CNN Staff*

**TIMBUKTU, Mali** — Across the shimmering sands of the Sahel, one of the world's most remarkable elephant populations is walking toward an uncertain future. Known as the "Desert Elephants of Mali" or the "Last Elephants of Timbuktu," this dwindling herd represents one of only two desert-adapted elephant populations remaining on Earth.

Each year, the herd traces a path dictated entirely by the search for water and vegetation, moving in a loop that takes them near communities and across increasingly contested terrain.

"These elephants have adapted to survive where few others could," explains a researcher familiar with the population. "Their migration is a marvel of endurance, but it also brings them into repeated contact with people and danger."

The animals typically travel in the cooler hours, conserving energy in an environment where temperatures can be brutal and water sources are scattered and seasonal.

## A Herd Under Siege

Multiple threats have converged on the elephants, driving their numbers dangerously low:

- **Poaching:** The illegal ivory trade has taken a devastating toll, with armed poachers exploiting regional instability to target the animals.
- **Regional Insecurity:** Ongoing conflict and the presence of armed groups in northern Mali have made conservation and monitoring efforts extraordinarily dangerous.
- **Climate Pressure:** Prolonged droughts and shrinking water sources strain a population already living at the edge of survival.
- **Human-Wildlife Conflict:** As people and elephants compete for the same scarce resources, tensions and dangerous encounters increase.

## A Call for Urgent Action

Conservation organizations and local partners are appealing for international support, emphasizing that protecting these elephants requires more than anti-poaching patrols—it demands the cooperation of local communities who share the land.

Programs that employ local people as guardians and eco-guards have shown promise, turning residents into stewards of the herd's survival. Advocates argue that the elephants' fate is deeply tied to the well-being and stability of the surrounding communities.

"Saving these elephants means investing in the people who live alongside them," one conservation advocate said. "It cannot be one without the other."

## What Comes Next

The story of Timbuktu's last elephants is, in many ways, a story about resilience—both of the animals and of the people determined to save them. Whether this ancient migration continues for future generations may depend on decisions made far beyond the desert's edge.

For now, the herd walks on, tracing a path their ancestors have followed for centuries, uncertain of what lies ahead.

# Dying of Thirst: Mali's Ancient Desert Elephants Face Their Gravest Threat

*As drought grips the Sahel, one of Earth's most remarkable elephant populations teeters on the edge of survival*

---

**GOURMA, Mali** — In the vast, sun-scorched expanse of Mali's Gourma region, where the Sahara Desert bleeds into the semi-arid Sahel, a herd of elephants moves slowly across cracked earth. Their journey—an ancient migration spanning hundreds of miles—has sustained them for millennia. Now, conservationists warn, it may be leading them toward extinction.

Photographs released this week by the Mali Elephant Project show emaciated adults shielding calves from the merciless sun, gathering at shrinking waterholes reduced to little more than mud. In one image that has circulated widely among conservation networks, a young elephant stands beside the sun-bleached bones of another that did not survive the dry season.

"These are among the last desert-adapted elephants on the planet," said Dr. Susan Canney, director of the Mali Elephant Project, in a statement accompanying the photos. "They have survived droughts before by following the rains across a landscape they know intimately. But what we are witnessing now is different—the water simply isn't coming back."

## The Longest Walk

Mali's Gourma elephants are extraordinary. Numbering perhaps 250 to 350 individuals, they undertake the longest known elephant migration on Earth, tracing a roughly circular route of nearly 400 miles in search of water and forage. They are supremely adapted to hardship, surviving in conditions that would kill their savanna cousins.

But adaptation has its limits.

Successive failed rainy seasons have devastated the region's fragile network of seasonal lakes and waterholes. The elephants, already pushed to their physiological edge, now travel farther between water sources—expending precious energy reserves that the youngest and oldest cannot spare.

"An elephant needs upwards of 40 gallons of water a day," explained a wildlife biologist working in the region who requested anonymity due to security concerns. "When the distances between water points stretch too far, the calves are the first to fail. We are seeing mortality that should alarm anyone who cares about this species."

## A Land of People and Pressure

The elephants' plight cannot be separated from the human story unfolding around them. Mali ranks among the least developed nations on Earth, sitting near the bottom of the United Nations Human Development Index. More than 40 percent of its people live in poverty, and the Sahel's communities face chronic food insecurity, limited access to clean water, and the compounding pressures of a warming climate.

For the herders and farmers who share the Gourma with the elephants, drought is not an abstraction—it is a daily fight for survival. Livestock die. Wells run dry. And in the competition for dwindling water, the interests of humans and elephants increasingly collide.

The region's difficulties are magnified by years of insecurity. Armed groups operate across northern and central Mali, displacing communities and making conservation work perilous. Rangers and researchers navigate not only environmental catastrophe but genuine physical danger.

"You cannot protect elephants without standing alongside the people who live with them," Dr. Canney has long argued. The Mali Elephant Project has pioneered a model that employs local youth, supports sustainable resource management, and gives communities a stake in the elephants' survival. In a fractured region, the elephants have become an unlikely symbol of common ground.

## A Race Against the Sun

Conservationists are now working urgently to identify and protect remaining water sources, and to support the pastoral communities whose fate is bound to the same parched land. But resources are scarce, access is difficult, and the climate is unforgiving.

"These animals have walked this land longer than any of us can imagine," the biologist said quietly. "To lose them now, on our watch, because the rains failed and the world looked away—that would be a tragedy we could never undo."

As the dry season deepens, the herd moves on, searching the horizon for water that may not be there. The photographs released this week are, in their way, a plea—an invitation to witness a vanishing world, and perhaps, to act before the last of Mali's desert giants fall silent beneath the Sahelian sun.
